lead: A second-order linear ODE can look harmless until a power series is tried and the coefficients misbehave at the chosen point. This chapter sorts each point into ordinary, regular singular, or irregular singular before any series is written. The label picks the method: plain Taylor series at an ordinary point, Frobenius series at a regular singular point, and no simple series at an irregular one. The same labels appear in heat flow, vibrating drums, and electric fields, where Bessel and Legendre equations put singular points at the edge of the useful interval.
prereq: You need Unit 2, Higher Order Linear ODEs and basic Taylor series from calculus.

sections.h3: Standard form and the three labels

blocks.text: Every second-order linear homogeneous ODE can be written in standard form. Here y is the unknown function of x; y′ and y″ are its first and second derivatives; P(x) and Q(x) are known coefficient functions.

blocks.where: P(x) is the coefficient of y′ after the y″ coefficient is made 1; Q(x) is the coefficient of y; both are functions of x only.

blocks.text: A point x₀ is ordinary when P and Q are analytic at x₀. Analytic means the function has a convergent Taylor series in powers of (x − x₀) around x₀. If either coefficient fails this test, x₀ is singular. Singular is not a verdict of uselessness. It says the plain power series y = Σ aₙ(x − x₀)ⁿ may fail, so the type of blow-up must be inspected.

items: Ordinary point: P and Q analytic at x₀.
Regular singular point: a singular point whose blow-up is mild, defined in the next section.
Irregular singular point: singular but not regular.
Some syllabi say regular point for ordinary point, and regular singularity for regular singular point.

blocks.text: At an ordinary point, a plain Taylor series is the natural trial; see 3.2 Power series solutions about an ordinary point.

At a singular point x₀, multiply P by one power of (x − x₀) and Q by two powers. If both products have finite limits as x → x₀, the point is regular singular. Equivalently, both products are analytic at x₀. The limits get their own symbols because they drive the indicial equation in 3.3 Frobenius method.
p₀ = lim (x→x₀) (x − x₀)P(x),   q₀ = lim (x→x₀) (x − x₀)²Q(x)
blocks.where: p₀ and q₀ are finite numbers when x₀ is a regular singular point; P and Q are the standard-form coefficients; the limit is taken along x ≠ x₀.

blocks.text: The powers are not arbitrary. They allow P to blow up no faster than 1/(x − x₀) and Q no faster than 1/(x − x₀)². A stronger blow-up makes the point irregular singular. A finite limit is enough; the function need not be defined exactly at x₀, because the limit ignores that one point.
Use this order every time: write standard form, test analyticity, then test the two limits only if the point is singular.

Bessel's equation of order ν is given below. Divide by x²: P(x) = 1/x and Q(x) = (x² − ν²)/x². At x = 0 both blow up, so x = 0 is singular. Then xP = 1 and x²Q = x² − ν², giving finite limits p₀ = 1 and q₀ = −ν². Hence x = 0 is a regular singular point. The solution is built in 3.5 Bessel functions.

blocks.where: ν is the order, a fixed real number; y″ and y′ are derivatives with respect to x.

blocks.text: Legendre's equation is (1 − x²)y″ − 2xy′ + n(n+1)y = 0. Standard form gives P(x) = −2x/(1 − x²) and Q(x) = n(n+1)/(1 − x²). At x = 1, both blow up. Compute (x − 1)P = 2x/(x + 1) and (x − 1)²Q = −n(n+1)(x − 1)/(x + 1). The limits are p₀ = 1 and q₀ = 0, so x = 1 is regular singular. The same check at x = −1 gives p₀ = 1 and q₀ = 0, so x = −1 is also regular singular. The polynomial solutions are in 3.4 Legendre polynomials.

figure.caption: The flowchart turns standard form into one of the three labels. Notice that regularity is tested only after a point is found singular.

spec.title: Classifying x₀
spec.aria: A flowchart starts with a point x₀ and sends the ODE to ordinary point or to a regularity check for singular points.

examples.question: Classify x = 0 and x = 1 for (x² − 1)y″ + xy′ + y = 0. Also state what happens at x = −1.
steps: Write standard form: divide by x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1). P(x) = x/(x² − 1), Q(x) = 1/(x² − 1).
At x = 0, x² − 1 = −1 ≠ 0. P(0) = 0 and Q(0) = −1, and both are analytic near 0. So x = 0 is an ordinary point.
At x = 1 the denominator is zero, so the point is singular.
(x − 1)P(x) = (x − 1)x/[(x − 1)(x + 1)] = x/(x + 1), which is analytic at x = 1. Its limit is p₀ = 1/2.
(x − 1)²Q(x) = (x − 1)²/[(x − 1)(x + 1)] = (x − 1)/(x + 1), which is analytic at x = 1. Its limit is q₀ = 0. So x = 1 is a regular singular point.
At x = −1, (x + 1)P(x) = x/(x − 1) and (x + 1)²Q(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 1). Both are finite at x = −1, with values 1/2 and 0. So x = −1 is also regular singular.
examples.answer: x = 0 is an ordinary point; x = 1 and x = −1 are regular singular points.

traps: Calling x = 1 irregular only because P and Q blow up. Regularity asks whether (x − x₀)P and (x − x₀)²Q stay finite.
Testing the original y″ coefficient instead of first dividing to standard form. P and Q are read only after the y″ coefficient is 1.
Swapping the factors: P gets one power of (x − x₀), Q gets two. The reverse test gives wrong labels.
Forgetting that a finite limit is enough at a singular point. The coefficient need not be defined exactly at x₀; the limit can remove a removable blow-up.
Treating ordinary and regular as the same word. Ordinary means P and Q are analytic; regular describes a mild singular point.

quiz.q: Define an ordinary point of y″ + P(x)y′ + Q(x)y = 0.
quiz.a: A point x₀ is ordinary when P(x) and Q(x) are both analytic at x₀, that is, each has a convergent Taylor series in powers of (x − x₀) around x₀.

quiz.q: Why can a regular singular point be attacked by a Frobenius series while an irregular singular point cannot by the same simple recipe?
quiz.a: At a regular singular point, P blows up at most like 1/(x − x₀) and Q at most like 1/(x − x₀)². Multiplying by (x − x₀)^r with a suitable r absorbs this mild blow-up. An irregular point has a stronger blow-up, so no single power removes it.
P(x) = 1/x and Q(x) = 1/x², so x = 0 is singular. xP = 1 and x²Q = 1, both finite. Hence x = 0 is regular singular with p₀ = 1 and q₀ = 1.

P(x) = 3x/(x² − 4), Q(x) = 1/(x² − 4). At x = 2, both blow up, so the point is singular. (x − 2)P = 3x/(x + 2) → 6/4 = 3/2; (x − 2)²Q = (x − 2)/(x + 2) → 0. So x = 2 is regular singular with p₀ = 3/2 and q₀ = 0.

quiz.q: At x₀, suppose (x − x₀)P(x) → ∞ and (x − x₀)²Q(x) → 0. What label fits, and why?
quiz.a: The point is irregular singular. The second limit is finite, but the first limit is infinite, so at least one of the two required limits fails. Regular singular needs both limits finite.

quiz.q: Show that Legendre's equation is regular singular at x = 1 and give p₀ and q₀.
quiz.a: For (1 − x²)y″ − 2xy′ + n(n+1)y = 0, P = −2x/(1 − x²), Q = n(n+1)/(1 − x²). At x = 1 both blow up. (x − 1)P = 2x/(x + 1) → 1, and (x − 1)²Q = −n(n+1)(x − 1)/(x + 1) → 0. Hence x = 1 is regular singular with p₀ = 1 and q₀ = 0.

quiz.q: Bessel's equation has a singular point at x = 0. Is it regular or irregular? Give p₀ and q₀.
quiz.a: It is regular singular. For x²y″ + xy′ + (x² − ν²)y = 0, P = 1/x and Q = (x² − ν²)/x². Then xP = 1 and x²Q = x² − ν², so p₀ = 1 and q₀ = −ν².

beyond: Not for the exam. The same classification extends to higher-order equations, where a singular point is regular if each coefficient blow-up is controlled by a suitable power. Frobenius theory at regular singular points is the gateway to hypergeometric equations, confluent hypergeometric equations, and asymptotic expansions near turning points. Search next for 'Frobenius method', 'regular singular point', 'indicial equation', and 'hypergeometric equation'.
